description.summary: A Japanese yōkai composed of smoke, said to dwell in bonfires and to be visible only to the pure of heart; first illustrated by Toriyama Sekien in the 1781 yōkai compendium Konjaku Hyakki Shūi.
description.full: Enenra (煙々羅) is a yōkai of Japanese folklore composed of smoke and darkness. Its name uses the kanji for 'smoke' (煙) doubled and joined with the character for thin gauze fabric (羅), evoking a spirit that drifts like sheer cloth on the air. Enenra reside in bonfires and similar wood-fires; when they emerge they take a vague humanoid shape within the rising smoke. They were introduced into the canonical yōkai bestiary by Toriyama Sekien in his 'Konjaku Hyakki Shūi' (今昔百鬼拾遺), the third book of his Gazu Hyakki Yagyō tetralogy, published c. 1781. Sekien's work appears to be loosely based on a passage in 'Tsurezuregusa' (the 14th-century Yoshida Kenkō essay collection) describing the smoke from summer mosquito-fires. According to subsequent commentary, an enenra can only be seen by those who are pure of heart. Two types are distinguished in later folklore literature: those born as enenra and (less commonly) the spirits of dead humans transformed into them. The enenra is generally treated as neutral or peaceful rather than malevolent.

etymology.origin: Japanese, coined or transmitted by Toriyama Sekien (1712–1788) in the late 18th century.
etymology.meaning: The kanji combine 'smoke' (煙) reduplicated with the character 羅, meaning a thin gauze fabric: 'thin-fabric of smoke', a poetic image of a spirit drifting like sheer cloth.
etymology.first_use: Konjaku Hyakki Shūi by Toriyama Sekien, c. 1781.

features.description: The enenra has no solid body; it is composed entirely of smoke, capable of taking momentary humanoid forms.
When emerging from a fire it can resolve into the silhouette of a human figure within the rising smoke.
Folklore states that only those of pure heart can perceive an enenra clearly.

physical.morphology: A non-corporeal being made of smoke; takes on transient humanoid forms but never possesses solid matter.

abilities.description: The yōkai is itself made of smoke and can pass freely with the smoke of fires.
Visible only to those of pure heart, and according to some later commentary, to those soon to die.
Lives within bonfires and other wood-fires, emerging with the rising smoke.

patterns: Manifests within the smoke of wood-fires
Generally peaceful or neutral toward humans
Departs as the fire dies down

range.description: Japanese folklore; the figure originates in Edo-period yōkai literature and is part of the contemporary national Japanese supernatural canon.

peak_activity_periods.description: Edo-period popularization through Sekien's published yōkai compendia
Revival within modern Japanese yōkai studies, manga, anime, and games

origins.cultural_roots: Edo-period Japanese yōkai tradition; Toriyama Sekien's compendia synthesized older folklore, classical literature, and original invention.
origins.earliest_accounts: First illustrated and named in Toriyama Sekien's 'Konjaku Hyakki Shūi' (c. 1781). The figure appears to be loosely inspired by a passage in the 14th-century 'Tsurezuregusa' of Yoshida Kenkō describing summer mosquito-fire smoke.
origins.folklore_connections: Part of the broader Edo-period imagination of yōkai associated with everyday objects and natural phenomena (smoke, dust, lanterns, hearths).

timeline.event: Toriyama Sekien publishes 'Konjaku Hyakki Shūi' (今昔百鬼拾遺), introducing the Enenra in illustration and short text
Death of Toriyama Sekien (1712–1788), author of the four Hyakki series including the volume that introduced Enenra
timeline.significance: Closes the foundational period of the figure

timeline.event: Matt Alt and Hiroko Yoda publish 'Japandemonium Illustrated: The Yokai Encyclopedias of Toriyama Sekien' (Dover, 2016, ISBN 978-0486800356), making Sekien's work, including Enenra, available in English translation

history.modern_era: Enenra is featured in modern yōkai reference works (Yokai.com, the GeGeGe no Kitarō franchise, Touhou Project, and others) and is treated as part of the canonical Japanese yōkai bestiary in scholarly and popular sources.

documentary.name: Konjaku Hyakki Shūi
documentary.description: Toriyama Sekien's illustrated yōkai compendium, the third book of his Gazu Hyakki Yagyō tetralogy, in which the Enenra is introduced.
documentary.analysis: Founding source; documents the figure's name, image, and brief description.

documentary.name: Japandemonium Illustrated
documentary.description: Annotated English translation of Sekien's four yōkai compendia, including the Enenra entry.
documentary.analysis: Standard contemporary English-language reference for Sekien's work.
documentary.source: Alt, M. & Yoda, H. (2016), Japandemonium Illustrated

paranormal.name: Yōkai of smoke
paranormal.description: Within Edo-period and modern yōkai discourse, the Enenra is treated as a real, if intangible, spirit native to bonfire smoke.
evidence_cited: Cohesive depiction across Sekien's work and later commentaries
Continuity with Japanese animistic conceptions of fire and smoke

skeptical.name: Sekien literary invention
skeptical.description: The Enenra is most plausibly a literary invention by Toriyama Sekien, loosely inspired by a passage in 'Tsurezuregusa' rather than by a pre-existing widespread folk tradition.
evidence_cited: No known earlier attestation than Sekien's 1781 compendium
Sekien's known practice of inventing yōkai based on classical phrases and word-play

skeptical.name: Pareidolia in smoke
skeptical.description: Apparent humanoid shapes in rising smoke are explained by ordinary perceptual pareidolia, codified into a stable folkloric figure by Sekien's illustration.
evidence_cited: Universality of human perception of figures in smoke and clouds
Fluid and indeterminate forms in Sekien's illustration

stories: The figure's appearance in bonfire smoke as illustrated by Sekien
The notion that an enenra can only be seen by the pure of heart
folklore.beliefs: Treated as a generally neutral or peaceful spirit, embodying the ephemeral and impermanent (a Buddhist resonance with mujō).
